title: What You Become Responsible For When You Open Your Own Florida Brokerage
metaDesc: An office, an entrance sign, branch registration, escrow reconciliation and every licensee under you. Florida attaches a set fine to each one you miss.
h1: What You Become Responsible For When You Open Your Own Florida Brokerage
about: The obligations a Florida broker takes on when opening a brokerage: maintaining a registered office and entrance sign under F.S. 475.22, registering branch offices under F.S. 475.24, escrow account reconciliation, corporate and officer registration, and the set fines the citation rule attaches to each failure.
answer: A physical office with a sign on it, a registration for every location, an escrow account you reconcile, and the licensing status of every person under you. Getting a broker license and opening a brokerage are different events, and the second one converts a long list of things that used to be someone else to worry about into your personal liability. Florida makes the list unusually easy to read, because the citation rule prints each administrative failure next to the fine it carries. Reading that list is the fastest honest preview of what the job actually involves.
takeaways: F.S. 475.22(1) requires a broker to maintain the required office and an office entrance sign. The citation rule sets $500 for failing to maintain the office and $100 for the missing sign.
F.S. 475.24 requires each additional location to be registered as a branch office. Failing to register one carries a $200 citation.

Escrow becomes yours. The rules require proper reconciliation of the escrow account, written permission from all interested parties before trust funds go into an interest bearing account, and the deposit and dispute clocks.

You become responsible for other people licensing status. Rule 61J2-5.019(1) covers failing to ensure the corporation or partnership is properly registered and that each officer, director and sales associate is properly licensed, at $500.
A sales associate or broker associate serving as an officer or director of a registered brokerage corporation is itself a listed violation at $200, which surprises people setting up an entity.
tldr: Opening your own firm moves a long list of administrative duties onto you personally: a registered office with a sign, a registration for every branch, a reconciled escrow account, and the licensing status of everyone under you. Florida publishes the price of getting each one wrong in its citation rule, which makes it the most honest job description available. Read it before you decide, not after.
body:
The broker license is the visible milestone. Opening a brokerage is the one that changes your life, and the two are frequently discussed as though they were the same decision.

Getting licensed is covered in how to get your Florida broker license. This page is about the part afterwards, and specifically about the obligations that arrive the day you have your own firm and your own licensees.

The most honest job description Florida publishes

There is an unusual document available to anyone considering this: the FREC citation rule. It lists administrative violations and prints the fine next to each one. It is not a guide to running a brokerage. It is better than that, because it is a list of the things people who run brokerages actually fail to do, compiled by the body that has to deal with them.

What follows is the part of that list a new broker should read twice. Amounts are set by rule and rules are amended, so read them for shape and seriousness rather than as a current price list.

A place, and a sign on it

F.S. 475.22(1) requires a broker to maintain an office and to have an entrance sign. The citation rule attaches $500 to failing to maintain the required office and $100 to failing to maintain the entrance sign.

The sign entry is the one people laugh at and then get caught by. It is an easy thing to overlook in a small suite or a shared building, and it is one of the few obligations here that a regulator can confirm by walking past.

Whether an office is worth having for commercial reasons is a separate argument, covered in whether a brokerage office still matters. The statutory question is not about whether it is useful.

Every location gets registered

F.S. 475.24 requires a location operating as a branch office to be registered as one. Failing to do that is a $200 citation. There is a separate entry at $500 for failing to register an out of state Florida broker office under F.S. 475.22(2).

This one grows teeth as a firm succeeds. The second location tends to open informally, out of momentum, and registration is the paperwork nobody owns.

The escrow account is now yours

This is the largest change and the one most under-weighted by agents moving up. Holding other people money is a trust obligation, and the rules around it are specific:

  • Reconciliation. The escrow account has to be properly reconciled. Failing to do so when the account balances is a $500 citation, and note the wording: the fine applies even where the account balances.
  • Timely deposits. Failing to immediately deposit trust funds is a listed violation, with a $200 citation available where the deposit is not more than three days late. The underlying deadlines are in how long a broker has to deposit earnest money.
  • Interest. Written permission from all interested parties is required before trust funds go into an interest bearing escrow account, at $300, and there is a further entry for failing to stop interest accruing before disbursement.
  • Disputes. When two parties claim the same deposit, the clocks and the four procedures in what happens when buyer and seller both claim the deposit become your personal responsibility, on business day deadlines.

You become responsible for other people

Rule 61J2-5.019(1) covers failing to ensure that the corporation or partnership is properly registered, and failing to ensure that each officer, director and sales associate is properly licensed. That is a $500 citation, and it is worth sitting with, because it means somebody else letting their license lapse becomes your violation.

There is a related trap for anyone structuring an entity: a sales associate or broker associate serving as an officer or director of a registered brokerage corporation is itself a listed violation at $200. People building a company around a team walk into that one while trying to be organized.

If the goal is leading people rather than owning the entity, the alternative is worth weighing honestly, and broker versus team leader and whether you need a broker license to run a team set out what you can do without taking any of this on.

Advertising, addresses and the small stuff

  • Advertising in a manner in which a reasonable person would not know they are dealing with a licensee or brokerage, or omitting the registered brokerage name: $500. The detail is in what Florida requires on your business cards, signs and social media.
  • Failing to timely notify the department of a current mailing address or a change to it: $500.
  • Using the name or identification of an association or organization while not in good standing or otherwise not entitled to it: $300.
  • Failing to include required information in a listing agreement, failing to give a copy to a principal within 24 hours, or including a self renewal clause: $200.

None of these are judgment calls. They are the operating overhead of being the responsible party, and they are the reason a brokerage needs an administrator far earlier than most founders plan for one.

The honest way to decide

Two questions, and the second is the real one.

First, do you want to own a firm, or do you want a bigger share of your own production? Those are different goals and only one of them requires any of this. The distinction is drawn out in the Florida career path from sales associate to broker.

Second, who does the administration? Every item above is a task with a deadline and a fine, and none of them generate a dollar. Founders who assume they will absorb it alongside a full personal production schedule are the ones who end up reading the citation rule for the first time in an envelope.

The short version

An office with a sign, every location registered, a reconciled escrow account on business day clocks, and the licensing status of everyone under you. Florida prints the price of each failure, which is the clearest preview of the job you will find anywhere. Read it before you decide.

faq.q: Do I need a physical office to run a Florida brokerage?
faq.a: F.S. 475.22(1) requires a broker to maintain the required office and an office entrance sign. The citation rule attaches $500 to failing to maintain the office and $100 to the missing entrance sign. Whether an office is commercially worth having is a separate question from whether the statute requires one.

faq.q: What happens if I open a second location?
faq.a: F.S. 475.24 requires a location operating as a branch office to be registered as one, and failing to do so carries a $200 citation. There is a separate $500 entry for failing to register an out of state Florida broker office under F.S. 475.22(2). Second locations tend to open informally, which is exactly how this gets missed.

faq.q: What changes about escrow when I am the broker?
faq.a: It becomes your personal responsibility. The account has to be properly reconciled, with a $500 citation for failing to do so even where the account balances. Trust funds must be deposited immediately, with a $200 citation available where a deposit is not more than three days late. Interest bearing accounts require written permission from all interested parties. And a disputed deposit puts you on business day deadlines with four statutory procedures to choose between.

faq.q: Am I responsible for whether my agents are properly licensed?
faq.a: Yes. Rule 61J2-5.019(1) covers failing to ensure the corporation or partnership is properly registered and that each officer, director and sales associate is properly licensed, at $500. In practice that means another person letting a license lapse becomes your violation, which is one of the largest differences between running a team and owning a firm.

faq.q: Can a sales associate be an officer of the brokerage corporation?
faq.a: It is a listed violation. Rule 61J2-5.016 covers a sales associate or broker associate serving as an officer or director of a registered brokerage corporation, at $200. People frequently walk into this while setting up a company structure around a team, which is a reason to take advice on the entity before filing anything.
